claims.text: The baseline material is a refractory high-entropy alloy composed of multiple high-melting refractory elements.
The baseline alloy lacks a targeted high-temperature strengthening phase.
The intervention is the addition of 2–3 atomic percent titanium to the baseline alloy.
Adding 2–3 atomic percent titanium will induce B2-phase formation.
The induced B2 phase will be nanoscale.
The induced B2 phase will be coherent with the matrix.
The induced B2 phase will form a continuous morphology.
The B2 phase will impede dislocation glide at elevated temperatures.
The B2 phase will impede grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures.
The titanium-modified alloy will have at least 50% higher high-temperature yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The titanium-modified alloy will exhibit at least a 50% improvement in creep resistance relative to the baseline alloy.
The predicted high-temperature improvements will hold during tensile and creep loading at 800–1200 °C.
Adding titanium will not significantly alter room-temperature ductility.
Adding titanium will not significantly increase the alloy density.
Minor titanium additions in similar alloy systems are known to promote B2 precipitation.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires at least a 50% improvement, whereas failure is defined only below a 30% improvement. A result between 30% and 49% would fail the stated prediction but would not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
